issues.body:
Profiling the agent loop on this machine (Ryzen 5 5560U, 6C/12T, MSYS2 MinGW64 GCC 16.1, Ninja + sccache + LLD) found two things that dominate edit-to-runnable time, neither of which is the compiler or the toolchain.

## 1. The exclusive shared build path serializes the machine

\dev.py\ mapped every worktree onto one machine-wide \subst\ drive under an exclusive lock, so that compile commands - and with them sccache cache keys - would be identical between worktrees.

Measured, with 9 worktrees on the box:

- a **0.8 s** no-op \
inja\ build took **215 s** wall, all of it waiting for the lock
- a repeat no-op build exceeded **300 s\\\

The lock bought cross-worktree cache sharing, but \SCCACHE_BASEDIR\ buys the same sharing without a lock: sccache rewrites paths under that directory to be relative before hashing, so two checkouts at different absolute paths produce the same key. Measured on one translation unit:

| | first compile | second, from a different root |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no \SCCACHE_BASEDIR\ | 6.41 s MISS | 6.36 s **MISS** |
| \SCCACHE_BASEDIR=<root>\ per checkout | 6.41 s MISS | 0.09 s **HIT** |

So: set \SCCACHE_BASEDIR\ to the worktree root and drop the subst drive and the lock. Worktrees build side by side with a shared cache. MAX_PATH is not a reason to keep the subst drive - the deepest path this tree produces is ~212 characters, in cargo's \	arget/\, and Windows 10+ long-path support handles it.

## 2. Unity builds are a net loss on a many-core machine

Unity cuts total work but collapses each group into **one un-parallelisable translation unit**, so the work it removes is paid back in lost parallelism. Same group built both ways:

| group | unity (1 TU) | per file (total CPU -> wall @ -j12) | single-file edit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| \Tactical\ (67 files) | 53.3 s | 263 s -> **21.9 s** (2.4x faster) | 50.1 s vs ~4 s |
| \sgp\ (43 files) | 28.7 s | 121 s -> **10.1 s** (2.9x faster) | 23.1 s vs ~3 s |

It also wrecks cache granularity: one 53 s cache entry covers 67 files, so editing any one of them invalidates all of it. Unity is a win on few-core machines and for release builds, so it becomes \-DENABLE_UNITY_BUILD=ON\, default \OFF\.

## What was checked and is NOT a problem

Answering the \\should we move off MinGW?\\ question with measurements rather than assumption:

- **Clang 22.1.8 vs GCC 16.1** on the same TU: 5.52 s vs 5.93 s = 0.93x, i.e. within noise on a contended box. No reason to port, and porting means rebuilding SDL3/FLTK/rmlui/sol2/gtest for clang.
- **Link** is ~2.5 s for the 184 MB \ja2.exe\ under LLD.
- **Unit tests**: 248 tests in ~12-17 s.
- **\-j12\ memory**: peak commit 18.7 G of a 40.3 G limit; safe.

## Definition of done

- [x] \SCCACHE_BASEDIR\ set by \dev.py\; shared build path, its lock and the subst mapping removed
- [x] \ENABLE_UNITY_BUILD\ added, default \OFF\, measured table in \COMPILATION.md\
- [x] \AGENTS.md\/\COMPILATION.md\ updated, including a note that the PCH win does not reproduce on GCC 16
- [x] unit tests, e2e (38/38) and the 1080p resolution suite (25/25) pass with unity off
issues.title: Build loop: stop serializing agents on a shared build path; make unity builds opt-in

issues.body:
## Context

The backlog's shape lives in GitHub, but GitHub cannot show it. Milestones group by increment, the board groups by track, and neither draws the interdependency between tasks — so "what is actually blocking me right now" and "which issues gate this one" are answered by reading ~200 issue bodies by hand.

The dependency information already exists in the repo, in prose. 144 of 211 issues reference other issues by `#N`, and a de-facto convention has grown up in the tactical revamp cluster:

> **Depends on:** #96, #260
> **Feeds:** #220, #108, #140
> **Gated by:** #263 (fixtures)
> **Unblocks:** #97, #98, #100, #101

Used in only 11 issues. Everywhere else, dependencies are loose sentences. So this issue is two things: give the graph a machine-readable source of truth, and render it.

The output is a **generated view of the issues, never a second copy**. Per AGENTS.md the board holds the issues, never its own copies; the same rule applies here. If the page and GitHub ever disagree, GitHub is right.

## What to build

### 1. Edges: use GitHub's native issue relations, not prose

GitHub has first-class issue dependencies, and `gh` exposes them:

```
gh issue view 102 --json blockedBy,blocking
gh issue edit 102 --add-blocked-by 96,260 --add-blocking 220,140
gh issue create --title ... --blocked-by 96
```

These render natively in GitHub's own issue sidebar, so declaring a dependency improves the GitHub page too. **That is the source of truth for edges** — one edge type, no parsing, no drift. It is currently unused on this backlog (0 relations set), which is why the graph has to be backfilled.

The four prose verbs map onto it:

| Prose verb | Native relation |
|---|---|
| `**Depends on:** #96, #260` | `blockedBy: 96, 260` |
| `**Gated by:** #263 (fixtures)` | `blockedBy: 263` — a gate is still a blocker |
| `**Feeds:** #220, #108` | the inverse: `blocking: 220, 108` |
| `**Unblocks:** #97, #98` | the inverse: `blocking: 97, 98` |

So the verbs collapse to one relation, and the parser's job becomes a **one-time backfill** rather than a permanent liability.

What prose keeps, and what the page must still read: the *nuance* the single relation cannot express — whether a blocker is a work item or a gate (a fixture, a proof, a decision), and why. Keep the `Depends on` / `Gated by` / `Feeds` lines in bodies as human-readable annotations, parse them **only** for those annotations, and never let them contradict the native relations.

Bare `#N` mentions outside one of these lines stay prose, not edges — too ambiguous to graph (#113's "Absorbed from #144" is a superseded reference, not a live blocker). The page shows them as a faint "mentions" count so the gaps stay visible.

Backfill scope: all 211 issues. The 11 with explicit verbs are mechanical; the rest need a judgement call per mention, so the backfill is a separate PR that touches only issue bodies and relations, is reviewable on its own, and reports every edge it created.

### 2. Generator

`tools/roadmap.py` (invoked as `python tools/dev.py roadmap`), pure stdlib, no new dependencies — the repo already runs on `uv` with Pillow/numpy and this must not add to that.

- Pulls issues (all states), milestones, labels, native `blockedBy`/`blocking`, and the board's `Track`/`Kind`/`Status` via `gh`.
- Caches to a committed `docs/roadmap/roadmap.json` snapshot so the page renders when `gh` is unavailable or rate-limited.
- Detects **cycles** and **dangling edges** (to a closed or non-existent issue) and reports them as warnings rather than failing. Both are expected on a hand-maintained backlog.
- Emits **one self-contained HTML file** — data inlined as JSON, no CDN, no build step, works offline from `file://`. Layout and colouring hand-written; no graph library vendored into the tree.
- Deterministic: same input → byte-identical output, so a regeneration diff is meaningful in review.

### 3. The page — three linked views

1. **Dependency DAG.** Nodes = issues, coloured by `Track`, edges = native relations, layered left→right by dependency depth. Closed issues dimmed, with a hide toggle. This is the view GitHub cannot produce.
2. **Milestone lanes.** One lane per milestone in milestone order, issues within a lane ordered by board status, with cross-milestone edges drawn over the lanes — so it is visible at a glance that, say, Tactical depth is gated on Testable Gameplay.
3. **Critical path / bottlenecks.** Over the *open* subgraph: the longest dependency chain, and the issues with the most open transitive dependents (the ones whose delay costs the most). Selected nodes highlight in the other two views.

Shared across all three: filter by track / status / label / milestone, text search, and a side panel with title, milestone, labels, dependency block, body, and a deep link to the issue.

### 4. Declaring dependencies without thinking about it

- **`python tools/dev.py dep <issue> --blocked-by #1,#2 --blocking #3`**, wrapping `gh issue edit` so an agent editing an issue updates the graph in one command, and `--clear` to drop them.
- **An issue form** (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`) whose `depends_on` field is applied by that helper after creation — GitHub's forms cannot set relations directly, so the template instructs creating the issue then running the helper. The form's help text documents the four verbs and the native relation.

### 5. Hosting

Orphan branch **`docs-site`**, served by GitHub Pages, pushed by a workflow with `workflow_dispatch` and a nightly schedule. Same reasoning as `pr-screenshots`: the page is generated output, so it must not enter `master`'s history and must not need a PR to refresh. Enable Pages for the repo once, pointing at `docs-site` / root.

The page shows its own generation timestamp and the issue count it was built from, so a stale page is obvious at a glance.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Backfill PR: every dependency currently expressed in prose is set as a native relation, and its report of created edges is reviewed. No contradiction left between prose and relations.
- [ ] `python tools/dev.py roadmap` emits `docs/roadmap/roadmap.html` from the live issues, with the committed JSON snapshot refreshed.
- [ ] Re-running with no GitHub changes produces a byte-identical file.
- [ ] All three views work on the real 211-issue backlog: DAG, milestone lanes with cross-lane edges, critical path / bottleneck highlighting.
- [ ] Filters (track, status, label, milestone), search and the side panel work; every node links to its GitHub issue.
- [ ] The page renders offline from `file://` with no network access.
- [ ] The issue form produces an issue whose relations the generator reads, verified end to end with a throwaway issue.
- [ ] `python tools/dev.py dep` adds and removes relations idempotently on a real issue.
- [ ] `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` documents the four verbs and the native relation; AGENTS.md's issues section points at the page.
- [ ] Cycle and dangling-edge detection reports clean, or today's real cycles are listed and understood.
- [ ] Pages enabled, `docs-site` published, workflow green on one manual run.
- [ ] PR carries a screenshot of the page — no game visual change, but the page is the deliverable.

## Non-goals

- Not a source of truth: no estimates, no assignments, no status editing, no comments. It reads GitHub and links back.
- No new runtime dependencies in the game build, and no vendored JS graph library.
- Not replacing the board. The board stays the ordering view; this is the dependency view.
- No estimates/Gantt — the repo carries no estimate data, and inventing a second number to plot would be noise.
- Sub-issues (parent/child) stay unused: milestones and the board already express grouping, and they would duplicate it.

## Open questions

- Should `docs/plan/*.md` also appear as nodes, so "write the plan doc" issues point at a real doc rather than only at each other?
- `Gated by` distinguishes a gate (fixture/proof/decision) from a work item. Should that become a label (`needs-fixture`, `needs-decision`) so the graph can style gates differently, or stay prose the page merely displays?

## Notes

- Track: Repo & CI. Kind: Task. Closes with the other loop work rather than as its own increment.
- Related: #53 set up the board/milestone conventions this page reads.

issues.body:
`WITH_ASAN` is defined in `src/CMakeLists.txt` but **cannot link on the Windows/MSYS2 toolchain**, so the option silently produces an unusable build.

## Evidence

With the current local toolchain (GCC 16.1, MSYS2 mingw64):

```
$ gcc -fsanitize=address -x c++ nul -o nul.exe
ld.exe: cannot find -lasan: No such file or directory
```

`libasan`, `libubsan` and `libtsan` are all absent from MSYS2 mingw64 (they live in the separate `-gcc-libs` packages, which are not installed). UBSan and TSan fail identically. So:

| | compile | link |
|---|---|---|
| ASan | OK | **fails** (`-lasan` missing) |
| UBSan | OK | **fails** (`-lubsan` missing) |
| TSan | **fails** | **fails** (`-ltsan` missing) |

## Why this matters

A developer who reads `src/CMakeLists.txt`, sees a supported `WITH_ASAN` option and turns it on gets a confusing link failure deep in a 492-TU build, or worse, a build that appears to work and produces no instrumentation. The codebase has a lot of legacy C-style memory handling and threads, so a working sanitizer is genuinely valuable â€” it is just not reachable from the platform most developers build on.

## Definition of done

- `WITH_ASAN` no longer claims to work where it cannot. Either it is removed, or it is documented as Linux/macOS-only and *fails at configure time with a clear message* on a toolchain that cannot link it.
- ASan **and** UBSan run in the Linux CI job on the game binary and/or the unit-test binary, so real defects get caught on every PR.
- The CI sanitizer run is not allowed to mask a failure: a non-zero exit or a sanitizer report fails the job.
- `docs/` or `COMPILATION.md` says plainly which platforms support sanitizers and why Windows/MinGW does not.

## Notes

- Per `AGENTS.md`, Rust is frozen â€” do not add sanitizers there.
- Keep sanitizer runs scoped so they do not blow the CI time budget; if the full binary is too slow under ASan, scope it to the unit-test binary and the fastest e2e tour rather than dropping it.

Closes nothing; relates to the other build-tooling issues in milestone 18.

issues.body:
The Linux CI job compiles with **GCC 10**, while local development uses **GCC 16.1**. That six-major-version gap means CI is the *oldest* thing in the loop, and it gates every other modernization step.

## Evidence

`.github/workflows/github-ci.yml` pins:

```yaml
env:
  CI_TARGET: ${{ matrix.cfg.target }}
  TARGET_GCC_MAJOR_VERSION: 10
```

`.ci/ci-setup.sh` then does `linux-install-via-apt-get gcc-10 g++-10` and `linux-set-gcc-version 10`. Locally, `gcc --version` reports 16.1.0 (MSYS2). Note that `coverity-scan.yml` already uses GCC 13, so the tree is not uniformly tested at 10 â€” it is *inconsistently* tested.

## Why this matters

Everything the team wants to adopt is blocked by this pin:

- **C++23 cannot be verified at all.** `-std=c++23` first exists in GCC 11. CI cannot prove a standard bump is green while it builds with GCC 10.
- Much of C++20 is too new or too slow to be worth using when the CI compiler is from 2021.
- New warning flags behave differently, or do not exist, on GCC 10.
- Bugs that only reproduce on a modern compiler ship silently.

A developer can build green locally on GCC 16 and have CI disagree. That is the expensive kind of drift.

## Definition of done

- `TARGET_GCC_MAJOR_VERSION` for the Linux job is raised to a modern release (14 or 16), and `ubuntu-22.04` is upgraded to a runner image that ships it.
- The `linux-mingw64` cross job is checked for the same staleness and brought into agreement where practical.
- The build passes on the new compiler **without** `-Wno-error` style suppression sweeping real problems under the rug; any warning that must be silenced is silenced deliberately and locally, with a comment.
- `min-rust-version`-style documentation records the minimum supported compiler, and `COMPILATION.md` is updated to match.
- Any GCC-10-only workaround in the tree is removed rather than carried forward.

## Notes

- Sequence matters: land this *before* the `-std=c++23` and new-warning-flags work, or those land untested.
- `AGENTS.md` asks for a measured approach on the dev loop; record the before/after build time so the change's cost is visible.

The build currently uses `-Wall -Wtype-limits -Wignored-qualifiers`. I measured what a broad set of additional flags actually fires on this tree, by recompiling a stratified sample of TUs straight from `_bin/compile_commands.json`. **18 flags are completely silent**, so they can be added for real bug-finding at zero cleanup cost.

## Measured â€” silent, add these now

On a 120-translation-unit sample stratified by file size:

```
-Wformat=2  -Wcast-qual  -Wnull-dereference  -Wduplicated-cond  -Wlogical-op
-Wunused  -Winit-self  -Wuninitialized  -Wstrict-aliasing=2  -Wparentheses
-Wimplicit-fallthrough  -Wcast-align  -Wpointer-arith  -Wwrite-strings
-Wjump-misses-init  -Wsizeof-pointer-memaccess  -Wnoexcept-type  -Wclobbered
```

Zero occurrences each. These catch format-string mistakes, qualifier casts, null dereferences, bad `memcpy` sizes and uninitialized reads â€” none of which `-Wall` reports.

## Measured â€” noisy, and what to actually do about it

| flag | hits | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `-Wpedantic` | 663 | **skip.** Essentially one header: `src/game/Tactical/Item_Types.h`, whose anonymous-union-of-anonymous-structs is a deliberate data-layout trick. Fixing it means rewriting a layout-sensitive struct â€” high risk, no value. |
| `-Wnon-virtual-dtor` | 226 | **fix â€” this is a real bug class.** See below. |
| `-Wredundant-decls` | 222 | fix, mechanical/scriptable. |
| `-Wswitch-enum` | 217 | **skip.** Pure noise. |
| `-Wunused-parameter` | 207 | **skip.** Noise; would need `[[maybe_unused]]` sprayed everywhere. |
| `-Wuseless-cast` | 140 | **skip.** Noise. |
| `-Wswitch-default` | 34 | skip. |
| `-Wdouble-promotion` | 19 | low value; skip for now. |
| `-Wshadow` | 17 | cheap enough to consider; `SOL`/`RmlUi` headers may contribute some. |
| `-Wfloat-equal` | 9 | skip; a game engine legitimately compares floats. |

## The one that matters: `-Wnon-virtual-dtor`

This is undefined behaviour, not style:

```
src/externalized/ItemSystem.h:15:7: warning: 'class ItemSystem' has virtual
    functions and accessible non-virtual destructor
src/externalized/MercSystem.h:8:7:   warning: 'class MercSystem' has virtual
    functions and accessible non-virtual destructor
src/externalized/ContentManager.h:67:7: warning: base class has accessible
    non-virtual destructor
```

`ItemSystem` and `MercSystem` are polymorphic base classes with public non-virtual destructors, and `ContentManager` derives from both. Deleting through a base pointer is UB.

## Definition of done

- The 18 silent flags are added to `add_warnings()` in `src/CMakeLists.txt`, and **CI compiles clean with them**.
- `ItemSystem` and `MercSystem` get a virtual (or `= default`, protected) destructor, verified against every derived type.
- `-Wnon-virtual-dtor` is enabled and the tree is clean, or any remaining case is individually justified in a comment.
- `-Wredundant-decls` is enabled and the duplicates removed.
- A short note in `src/CMakeLists.txt` records which flags were deliberately **not** enabled and why, so the next person does not re-litigate `-Wpedantic`.
- Nothing is silenced globally with a bare `-w` / `-Wno-everything`.

## Notes

- This depends on the CI-compiler-bump issue; GCC 10 does not have all of these.
- No new `-Werror` until the tree is clean â€” the goal is visibility, not a red build.

Part of the build-tooling set in milestone 18.

There is **no `.clang-format` and no `.clang-tidy` in the repository**. Rust already has `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -D warnings` in CI; C++ has nothing equivalent. Meanwhile `clang-format` 22.1.8 is already installed on the dev machine but unused.

## Definition of done

### `.clang-format`

- A config committed at the repo root, matching the code as it actually looks today (tabs, brace style, 120-col-ish) â€” **not** a wholesale reformat.
- Formatting is verified in CI on changed lines only, or is explicitly adopted as a separate mechanical commit. Do not mix reformatting into feature work.

### `.clang-tidy`

- `mingw-w64-x86_64-clang-tools-extra` (157 MB, clang 22.1.8 â€” clang itself is already installed) provides `clang-tidy`. Add it to the documented MSYS2 package list.
- A committed `.clang-tidy` with a **small, high-value** check list rather than everything: a handful of `bugprone-*`, `performance-*` and the specific `modernize-*` checks this tree actually benefits from.
- Config accounts for the vendored/generated headers (`sol2`, `lua`, `miniaudio`, `RmlUi`, `gtest`, `string_theory`) via `HeaderFilterRegex`, so third-party headers produce no noise.
- Runs in CI **on the pull-request diff only** (`clang-tidy-diff.py` / `--line-filter`), because a full-tree run over 492 TUs is too slow and far too noisy to be a gate.
- Findings that are known-unfixable in legacy code are handled with targeted `NOLINT` + a comment, not by weakening the check.

### Cheap win already available

- `clang-format` alone, applied to new and changed code, is most of the consistency benefit at near-zero cost. Ship that even if the tidy work slips.

## Notes

- Do **not** add a clang-format reformat of the whole tree into the same PR as the config; the diff would bury the real change.
- `AGENTS.md` prefers a short feedback loop. If full-tree tidy is too slow to be useful, say so in the config and keep it diff-scoped rather than making it everyone's build.

Probing 56 translation units with `-std=c++23` on the local GCC 16.1 produced **zero errors and zero new warnings**. The standard switch is essentially free today.

## Evidence

```
$ ... -std=c++23 -fsyntax-only   # over 56 stratified TUs
candidate TUs: 56
total warning: lines = 0   total error: lines = 0
```

`CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20` and `target_compile_features(${JA2_BINARY} PRIVATE cxx_std_20)` both say C++20; neither mentions 23. The standard is declared in two places that must move together.

## Adoption measured in the tree

| feature | uses | |
|---|---|---|
| `std::span` | 9 | barely adopted, good API |
| `std::optional` | 63 | adopted |
| `std::variant` | 7 | barely adopted |
| `std::string_view` | 20 | barely adopted |
| `std::ranges` | 0 | not adopted |
| `std::format` | 0 | see caveat |
| `operator<=>` | 0 | |
| `if const` init-statement | 0 | |
| `std::to_underlying` | 0 | free win |
| `std::bit_*` | 0 | free win |
| `constexpr` | 477 | well adopted |
| `auto` variables | 1601 | well adopted |
| generic lambdas | 12 | |

## What to adopt, and what to skip

**Adopt:**
- `std::expected<T,E>` — the single biggest win. It removes the codebase's out-parameter result pattern (`bool LoadX(Out* out)`). It is the idiomatic choice on all three toolchains and needs no migration of the rest of the code.
- `std::to_underlying` — trivial one-liners, currently zero uses.
- `std::byteswap`, `std::unreachable`, `std::string::contains`, `std::move_only_function` — small, safe, local.
- `std::span` and `std::ranges::to` to finish the job the 9 `std::span` uses started.

**Skip — and record why, so nobody re-proposes it:**
- **`std::format` is not the win it appears.** This tree uses `string_theory` **3658** times versus `std::string` 1400. Migrating to format-strings means a second standard library and a rewrite of the string surface, not a modernization. Do not open a `std::format` migration.
- **"Deducing this" / explicit object parameter**: compiles on GCC 14+/MSVC 17.13+, but has essentially zero production adoption anywhere. Not worth being the only project using it.
- `std::mdspan` (GCC 16 only) and `std::generator` (absent from the MSVC STL) are not portable across the toolchains this project builds on. Use `std::span` with stride arithmetic instead.

## Definition of done

- `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD` and `cxx_std_20` move to 23 **together**, with a comment saying why the duplication exists.
- The full CI matrix builds clean in C++23 mode on the bumped compiler.
- `std::expected` is used for at least the content/loader layer that currently returns `bool` + out-param; gtest coverage for it lands with it.
- `std::to_underlying` replaces the hand-written enum-to-int casts.
- A short note records the deliberate skips (`std::format`, deducing `this`, `mdspan`) and the reasoning.

## Notes

- **Blocked on the CI compiler bump**: GCC 10 cannot do `-std=c++23`. Land that first.
- MSVC has no `/std:c++23` — only `/std:c++latest` + `/std:c++23preview`. Anything adopted must be feature-tested behind `__cpp_lib_*` macros so the MSVC path keeps building.

Part of the build-tooling set in milestone 18.

issues.body:
The tree still uses `NULL` **2709 times across 240 of 997 files**. This is the last large mechanical legacy holdover and it is exactly the kind of change a linter should do for us.

## Evidence

`NULL` is the C macro. In C++ it should be `nullptr`: same null pointer value, but type-correct, not overloadable, not a macro, and not silently convertible to integer. Top files:

```
106  Handle_UI.cc        83  MapScreen.cc        79  Overhead.cc
 73  SoundMan.cc         68  Soldier_Control.cc  67  Turn_Based_Input.cc
 63  Sound_Control.cc    59  Interface_Items.cc  58  Handle_Items.cc
```

Already-clean baseline, for contrast: **zero** raw `new`/`delete`, **zero** `malloc`/`free`, **zero** C-style pointer casts beyond a handful, only 2 unsafe C string calls. The memory-management modernisation is essentially done; `NULL` is what remains. There are also 231 `goto`s, but those in this codebase are typically intentional loop exits and are *not* part of this issue.

## Definition of done

- `NULL` → `nullptr` across `src/`, done **mechanically**, in a commit that changes nothing else.
- Done with `clang-tidy -checks=-*,modernize-use-nullptr` (the tool that already arrives with the linting work) rather than by hand, so the transformation is reproducible.
- Covered: pointer initialisation, comparisons, returns, `= NULL` defaults, and macro/argument uses.
- Left alone, with a comment explaining why: `NULL` used as an *integer* sentinel where `nullptr` would change semantics — e.g. sentinel values in range loops, `0`-vs-`NULL` distinctions, or anything passed through a C API that documents `NULL`. A blind global replace is not acceptable; each exception is justified.
- Build, unit tests and the e2e suite pass. This is a large diff, so rely on the tests rather than on review-by-reading.

## Notes

- Keep this as its own PR. A 2700-line mechanical change is unreviewable when mixed with anything else.
- Succeeds the `-Wzero-as-null-pointer-constant` situation indirectly, but that flag is not being enabled — `NULL` is a macro, so the clean fix is `nullptr`, not a warning.
